Teen sleep — CDC general reference

For teenagers aged 13–17, CDC lists 8–10 hours of sleep daily as a general recommendation. Sleep quality also matters. Sleep difficulties or symptoms of a sleep disorder should be discussed with a healthcare provider. This reference is not an individualized basketball prescription or an adopted planning threshold.

Duration alone does not describe sleep quality.
Sleep problems and symptoms of a sleep disorder warrant healthcare-provider discussion.
Underlying citation: Paruthi S, Brooks LJ, D'Ambrosio C, et al. Recommended amount of sleep for pediatric populations: a consensus statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. J Clin Sleep Med. 2016;12(6):785–786.

Source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), About Sleep.
Use of CDC information and links does not imply endorsement by the United States Government, HHS, CDC, or ATSDR.
Preserve the source's substantive meaning, including its age range, daily reporting basis and sleep-quality and provider-context qualifications.
The underlying CDC material is freely available on the agency website: https://www.cdc.gov/sleep/about/.

required_delivery_record.display_text:
Passing options and outlet context

The UGA chapter distinguishes bounce, chest and overhead passes. It describes a bounce pass as reaching a teammate after contacting the floor, with a typical use when defenders have raised hands. A chest pass begins from the chest with both hands on the ball and a forward push from the chest; the chapter associates it with distance or speed. An overhead pass starts above the head and includes a forward follow-through. The chapter presents it as a common outlet option after a rebound, when the rebounder sends the ball to a teammate farther along the court. These are source-described technique and tactical examples.

General introductory basketball reference, selected and paraphrased from the cited chapter. No youth-specific suitability, training dose, medical clearance or planner approval is established.

Source: 2. Fundamentals – Passing, Ch.1 - Basketball, UGA PEDB Program. https://open.online.uga.edu/basketball/chapter/2-fundamentals-passing/

required_delivery_record.display_text:
Balance and shooting-hand roles

The UGA chapter presents balance as a foundation for shooting, particularly for beginners, and describes an approximately shoulder-width base. It assigns different roles to the hands: the dominant hand propels the ball while the other hand supports and guides it. The chapter connects aiming the shooting elbow toward the target with coordinated knee movement and bringing the ball into shooting position. Its follow-through explanation describes the ball leaving the fingertips and developing backspin.

General introductory basketball reference, selected and paraphrased from the cited chapter. No youth-specific suitability, training dose, medical clearance or planner approval is established.

Source: 4. Fundamentals – Shooting, Ch.1 - Basketball, UGA PEDB Program. https://open.online.uga.edu/basketball/chapter/fundamentals-shooting/

required_delivery_record.display_text:
Off-ball spacing and team context

The UGA chapter describes offensive spacing as distributing teammates so defenders are spread across the court. Positioning depends on the ball carrier and the opposing defense. When a teammate drives toward the basket, an off-ball player may have different options according to how the defense responds; helping create a score does not necessarily mean taking the shot personally. The chapter also connects effective positioning with learning teammates’ tendencies over time.

General introductory basketball reference, selected and paraphrased from the cited chapter. No youth-specific suitability, training dose, medical clearance or planner approval is established.

Source: 5. Fundamentals – Spacing & Rebounding, Ch.1 - Basketball, UGA PEDB Program. https://open.online.uga.edu/basketball/chapter/4-fundamentals-spacing-rebounding/

required_delivery_record.display_text:
Man-to-man defensive positioning

The UGA chapter introduces a positioning example for a defender facing an opponent with the ball in a man-to-man scheme. In that setting, it suggests noticing which hand the opponent prefers for dribbling and using positioning to discourage movement toward that preferred side. Its example concerns a right-handed ball handler and a defender trying to encourage movement to the other side. The example depends on the defensive strategy and the opponent’s tendencies. It is a source-described tactical concept, not a mandatory defense for every player or game.

General introductory basketball reference, selected and paraphrased from the cited chapter. No youth-specific suitability, training dose, medical clearance or planner approval is established.

Source: 6. Fundamentals – Defending, Ch.1 - Basketball, UGA PEDB Program. https://open.online.uga.edu/basketball/chapter/2-basketball-fundamentals-skills-and-techniques/

required_delivery_record.display_text:
Man-to-man, help-side and zone responsibilities

The UGA chapter distinguishes defensive responsibility for an assigned opponent from responsibility for an area. In man-to-man defense, a player guards a particular opponent while also helping teammates. Its help-side example describes a ball handler getting past a defender and driving toward an unguarded basket: the next closest defender moves to assist. For a zone defense, the selected definition assigns players to areas rather than to particular opponents.

General introductory basketball reference, selected and paraphrased from the cited chapter. No youth-specific suitability, training dose, medical clearance or planner approval is established.

Source: 7. Strategies, Ch.1 - Basketball, UGA PEDB Program. https://open.online.uga.edu/basketball/chapter/3-basketball-strategies/

required_delivery_record.display_text:
Controlled dribbling and court awareness

The UGA chapter emphasizes fingertip control rather than the palm and describes dribbling with one hand at a time. Keeping the head raised is presented as a way to notice defenders, teammates and surrounding space. The chapter also advises limiting unnecessary dribbling because a pass can move the ball forward quickly and create openings. Direction changes may involve a crossover, a behind-the-back movement or a transfer between the legs. Its central control concept is being able to handle the ball on either side and transfer it between hands while maintaining awareness.

General introductory basketball reference, selected and paraphrased from the cited chapter. No youth-specific suitability, training dose, medical clearance or planner approval is established.

required_delivery_record.display_text:
Youth daily activity and weekly activity mix

CDC's general recommendation for children and adolescents aged 6–17 is at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity each day. Most should be aerobic, with vigorous aerobic activity on at least three days each week. Muscle- and bone-strengthening activity are each included on at least three days weekly as part of the daily activity, rather than as separate additional sixty-minute blocks. Choices should be varied, age-appropriate and enjoyable.

Population-level activity guidance for ages 6–17. The daily amount covers the activity mix; the weekly components do not require separate additional sixty-minute sessions. This is not an individualized basketball workload or an adopted project planning threshold.

Source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Child Activity: An Overview.

required_delivery_record.display_text:
Youth activity intensity and the talk test

For children and adolescents aged 6–17, CDC describes the talk test as a general way to interpret activity intensity: moderate effort permits talking but not singing, while vigorous effort permits only a few words before a pause for breath. It notes that bicycling or basketball may occur at either intensity, so a sport's name alone does not determine the effort. Activities should be enjoyable, safe and appropriate for age and skill.

A general intensity description within youth physical-activity guidance, not a clinical test, a numeric heart-rate cutoff or a universal classification of every basketball session. It does not establish individual readiness or planner eligibility.

required_delivery_record.display_text:
Enjoyable activity routines and activity-specific safety

CDC encourages enjoyable physical activity, including structured and unstructured forms, family routines, access to equipment and places to be active, and positive encouragement. Activities should fit the child's age. Its safety discussion gives helmets or pads for activities such as cycling, scooter riding, skating and rock-wall climbing as examples of protective equipment. Those examples are activity-specific, not a statement that every sport uses the same equipment.

General encouragement and activity-specific safety context. This does not approve a catalog exercise, establish an individual training dose or replace sport-specific supervision and equipment review.

Disability context and experienced professional guidance

In its section about children with disabilities, CDC advises discussing a physical-activity routine with a doctor before starting and seeking guidance from a professional experienced in physical activity and disability. That advice concerns amounts and types of activity appropriate to the child's abilities. The section-specific context must remain attached; it is not a universal medical-clearance requirement for every child.

Preserve the disability-section scope. This reference neither diagnoses a condition nor grants medical clearance or planner eligibility, and it does not adopt a project-wide restriction on all children.
